title: Derivatives
tagline: Forwards and futures, swaps, option payoffs and arbitrage bounds, binomial trees, the Black–Scholes model, the Greeks and hedging, numerical methods, credit derivatives and risk measurement
summary: Derivatives — contracts whose value depends on the price of something else — are used to transfer risk, to take positions, and to complete markets, and they played a central part in the financial crisis of 2008. This course prices them by no-arbitrage: forwards, futures and swaps, option payoffs and bounds, binomial trees, the Black–Scholes model and its Greeks, dynamic hedging and numerical methods, credit derivatives, and the measurement and management of financial risk.
overview: A **derivative** is a contract whose payoff is a function of something else: a share price, an interest rate, an exchange rate, a commodity, or a credit event. The something else is the **underlying**. The economic function of the contract is to unbundle risks that would otherwise travel together. A miller who will buy wheat in six months, and a farmer who will harvest it, can lock a price today with a forward; neither needs to guess the harvest-time spot. A bank that has lent at a floating rate and funded itself at a fixed rate can swap the two. An airline that will buy jet fuel, and a producer who will sell it, can share the price risk without merging the firms. The same contracts can be used to take a view rather than to offset one. The course explains how the contracts work and how no-arbitrage prices them. It does not recommend that anyone hedge, speculate, or leave a risk unhedged.

The organising idea is **replication**. If a portfolio of traded assets matches the derivative's payoff in every state, the derivative's price today must equal the portfolio's cost today, or an arbitrageur could buy the cheap side and sell the dear side. For forwards, futures and swaps the replicating portfolio is static: hold the underlying, borrow or lend, and wait. For options it is dynamic: the mix of underlying and cash has to be rebalanced as the underlying moves. The one-step binomial tree makes that rebalancing visible by hand. The multi-step tree, taken to a continuous-time limit under extra assumptions, produces the Black–Scholes–Merton formula. The **Greeks** are the derivatives of that formula; they are the recipe for the hedge and the diagnosis of what the hedge leaves behind. When the formula does not apply — American exercise, barriers, path dependence, jumps — one turns to trees, finite differences and Monte Carlo, each with a stated error.

Two further chapters treat default and risk measurement. A credit default swap is a swap whose floating leg is a default; its spread is a market quote for a survival probability once a recovery assumption is named. Value at risk is a quantile of a loss distribution. It is a statistic, not a safety certificate: it is silent about the size of losses beyond the quantile, it is only as good as the distribution that was fed to it, and several crises have been, in part, a reminder of that silence. The course is for education. Every numerical example uses illustrative values ($S = 100$, $K = 100$, $r = 0.05$, $\sigma = 0.20$ and close cousins). Historical statistics carry a source and a date and are not a forecast.

The course is hard in three places. First, no-arbitrage is a *relative* pricing method: it prices a derivative given the underlying, the rate and (for options) a volatility; it does not say what the underlying itself is worth. Second, the Black–Scholes world — lognormal prices, no jumps, continuous frictionless hedging — is a model, and implied volatility is the number that makes the model match a quote, not a promise that the assumptions hold. Third, risk numbers compress a distribution to a few statistics; reading them without the assumptions is the usual source of false comfort. Work every tree by hand before taking a limit, state the assumptions of every formula you use, and treat a VaR as a description of a model, not as a bound on the world.
outcomes: Price a forward or futures contract by cash-and-carry replication, and adjust the cost-of-carry formula for dividends, storage and foreign interest.
Value a plain vanilla interest-rate swap from a discount curve, and interpret the swap rate as a par yield.
Draw option payoffs and combinations, derive put–call parity, and prove the model-free no-arbitrage bounds on European calls and puts.
Replicate a European option on a one- and two-step binomial tree, compute the risk-neutral probability, and price an American put by backward induction.
State the Black–Scholes–Merton assumptions, obtain the formula as a binomial limit and from the hedging PDE, and compute a European call and put from $S$, $K$, $r$, $\sigma$ and $T$.
Compute delta, gamma, vega, theta and rho, and explain what a discrete delta-hedge leaves unhedged.
Price a European claim by Monte Carlo under the risk-neutral measure, and outline a finite-difference scheme for the Black–Scholes PDE.
Relate a credit spread to a hazard rate and a recovery rate, and value a credit default swap in a reduced-form model.
Compute Gaussian value at risk and expected shortfall for an illustrative portfolio, and explain why VaR is a statistic rather than a bound on losses.

chapters.summary: Forward and futures contracts, margining, cost-of-carry pricing and the minimum-variance hedge ratio.

chapters.summary: Interest-rate and currency swaps, the par swap rate, and valuation from a discount curve.

chapters.title: Options: payoffs and arbitrage bounds

chapters.title: The binomial model
chapters.summary: One- and multi-period binomial trees, replication, risk-neutral valuation, American exercise and the continuous-time limit.

chapters.title: The Black–Scholes model
chapters.summary: Lognormal prices, the Black–Scholes–Merton formula as a binomial limit and from the hedging argument, and implied volatility.

chapters.summary: Delta, gamma, vega, theta and rho, the Black–Scholes PDE identity, and discrete hedging error.

chapters.summary: Monte Carlo under the risk-neutral measure, finite-difference methods, and path-dependent options.

chapters.title: Credit risk and credit derivatives

chapters.title: Risk measurement and management

history.title: The Chicago Board of Trade
history.detail: The Chicago Board of Trade was organised on 3 April 1848 as a cash market for grain. Forward or “to-arrive” contracts began to trade there almost at once, giving Midwestern harvests a centralised price before the modern futures contract existed.

history.title: Standardised futures at the CBOT
history.detail: On 13 October 1865 the Chicago Board of Trade adopted formal trading rules on margin and delivery. Those rules are the usual marker for the shift from bespoke forwards to standardised, exchange-traded futures.

history.title: Listed options and the Black–Scholes formula
history.detail: The Chicago Board Options Exchange opened on 26 April 1973, listing call options on sixteen shares. In May–June 1973 Fischer Black and Myron Scholes published “The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities” in the Journal of Political Economy; Robert C. Merton’s “Theory of Rational Option Pricing” appeared the same year in the Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science.

history.title: The binomial option-pricing model
history.detail: John C. Cox, Stephen A. Ross and Mark Rubinstein published “Option Pricing: A Simplified Approach” in the Journal of Financial Economics, giving a discrete-time replicating tree whose limit is Black–Scholes and which prices American exercise by backward induction.

history.title: The IBM–World Bank currency swap
history.detail: In August 1981 Salomon Brothers arranged a currency swap between IBM and the World Bank: the Bank issued dollars and took over IBM’s Swiss-franc and Deutsche-mark obligations. The trade is the conventional starting point of the modern swap market.

history.title: RiskMetrics and value at risk
history.detail: In October 1994 J.P. Morgan released RiskMetrics, a documented variance–covariance methodology and a public data set for computing value at risk. VaR became a standard internal and regulatory statistic; its limits were already visible in the fine print of the technical document.

history.title: The Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences
history.detail: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel was awarded to Robert C. Merton and Myron S. Scholes “for a new method to determine the value of derivatives”. Fischer Black, who had died in 1995, was named in the citation but the Prize is not awarded posthumously.

history.title: Credit derivatives in the financial crisis
history.detail: Lehman Brothers filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on 15 September 2008. Credit default swaps and related structured credit products transmitted losses through the dealer network; AIG’s CDS book required official support. The episode is the leading case for treating counterparty risk, collateral and model risk as part of the derivative, not as an afterthought.

references.title: Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives
references.note: Eleventh edition. The standard undergraduate and master’s text: contract mechanics, no-arbitrage pricing, trees, Black–Scholes, Greeks, credit and risk measures, with many numerical examples.

references.title: Derivatives Markets
references.note: Third edition. Careful on replication, binomial pricing and the link to the stochastic discount factor; a natural companion to the asset-pricing course.

references.title: The Mathematics of Financial Derivatives
references.authors: Paul Wilmott, Sam Howison and Jeff Dewynne
references.note: A PDE-first treatment of Black–Scholes, the Greeks and finite-difference methods, written for readers who want the equations rather than the term sheet.

references.title: Stochastic Calculus for Finance II: Continuous-Time Models
references.note: The standard mathematically honest development of Brownian motion, the Black–Scholes derivation and change of measure, after the discrete-time first volume.

references.title: Value at Risk: The New Benchmark for Managing Financial Risk
references.note: Third edition. The workhorse account of VaR, mapping, backtesting and the institutional history of the statistic.

references.title: Quantitative Risk Management
references.authors: Alexander J. McNeil, Rüdiger Frey and Paul Embrechts
references.note: Second edition. Heavy-tailed losses, copulas, expected shortfall and credit portfolios; the place to go once Gaussian VaR is no longer enough.

references.title: Dynamic Asset Pricing Theory
references.note: Third edition. Arbitrage, state prices and the martingale method in continuous time, including term-structure and credit models.

references.title: Financial Calculus: An Introduction to Derivative Pricing
references.note: A short, clean introduction to discrete then continuous no-arbitrage pricing, useful as a first pass before Shreve or Duffie.
